title: AI assistance and algorithmic management expand faster than evidence of worker control
source_unit: Deliberately non-pooled comparison of worker/task experiments, employer algorithmic-management reports, executive expectations, and CPS union representation
geography: United States with comparative OECD employer-survey context and four-country executive survey

denominator.unit: customer-support agents in 2023 field experiment; companion studies have separate denominators of 7,137 knowledge workers, 13,920 RPS workers, and 1,174 experimental participants

knowledge_worker_email_time.unit: hours per week among treated users in second half of six-month experiment

within_occupation_or_task_adoption.value: fewer than half in most occupations and tasks

observations.method: Bounded comparison of NBER field experiments, nationally representative worker/task survey evidence, and a randomized online task experiment; units and interventions are not pooled.
observations.uncertainty: Productivity and time effects are study-specific; saved time may be reallocated by employers, worker adoption is not workplace exposure, and task performance is not pay, promotion, autonomy, health, or bargaining power.
observations.subgroup: Customer-support agents, knowledge workers, workers within occupations/tasks, and adults grouped by education in separate studies.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI can assist lower-skilled workers or narrow a task-performance gap while employers retain allocation, evaluation, monitoring, and pay authority; lower email time is not automatically worker-controlled time.

observations.period: June-August 2024; OECD employer survey algorithmic-management context

denominator.unit: firms with 20 or more employees across six countries; US country rates have separate weighted item universes

us_firms_with_at_least_one_algorithmic_m.unit: percent of US firms reported by managers

us_firms_with_ten_or_more_tools.unit: percent of US firms reported by managers

us_firms_monitoring_conversation_content.unit: percent of US firms reported by managers

users_with_worker_impact_concern.unit: share of algorithmic-management users across six countries

users_with_governance_measure.unit: percent of algorithmic-management users across six countries

observations.method: OECD representative employer survey comparison; algorithmic management includes software that instructs, monitors, or evaluates workers and is broader than generative AI.
observations.uncertainty: Manager reports measure provision and perceptions, not worker exposure, consequential use, consent, enforcement, remedy, or independent audit quality. Country composition and legal contexts differ.
observations.subgroup: US firms with 20 or more employees and six-country algorithmic-management users; manager/supervisor perspective.
observations.counterinterpretation: Administrative or scheduling tools may have limited consequences; a governance measure or worker consultation can exist without effective contestability or power to change a decision.

observations.period: 2026; executive firm survey covering prior and expected next three years

denominator.unit: nearly 6,000 senior business executives in the US, UK, Germany, and Australia

no_past_three_year_firm_employment_or_pr.unit: percent of executives reporting no impact

expected_next_three_year_productivity_ch.unit: percent average expected increase at own firm

observations.method: NBER executive survey comparison of current use, retrospective firm effects, and forward expectations; employer and employee expectation measures are retained separately.
observations.uncertainty: Executive perceptions and expectations are not realized administrative outcomes, and the four-country sample is not a US-only estimate. Occupation, implementation rules, pay, hours, and bargaining outcomes are unobserved.
observations.subgroup: Senior executives; younger and more productive firms report higher usage; employer and employee expectation perspectives differ.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low retrospective impact can coexist with future reorganization, while expected productivity need not reach workers or households; expectation gaps can reflect information or incentive differences rather than realized conflict.

observations.period: 2024-2025; US formal union membership and representation context

denominator.unit: thousand employed wage and salary workers in 2024; 2025 denominator is 146,661 thousand

observations.method: BLS CPS annual-average Table 1; represented workers include members and workers covered by a union or employee-association contract.
observations.uncertainty: The 2025 annual estimate excludes October because of the federal shutdown and is not strictly comparable with other annual averages. Formal representation is not a direct measure of schedule control, appeal, autonomy, or AI exposure.
observations.subgroup: Employed wage and salary workers age 16 or older; self-employed workers excluded.
observations.counterinterpretation: A small movement in formal coverage cannot establish practical bargaining power, and low coverage does not mean workers lack informal voice or alternative institutions.

related_sources.claim: NBER worker/task and workplace experiments provide the adoption, time, productivity, and performance stages.
OECD provides employer-reported algorithmic-management adoption and governance context.
NBER provides executive retrospective and forward expectation evidence.

boundary: This is a non-pooled AI-at-work and worker-voice bridge. It establishes selected adoption, productivity/time, employer-governance, executive-expectation, and formal-representation surfaces. It does not establish worker exposure, realized employment or pay effects, autonomy, bargaining power, household security, cultural meaning, political response, or geopolitical leverage. A common workplace event with monitoring, training, discretion, appeal, representation, and later outcome remains open.
